strengths: Clear problem identification with well-motivated limitations of black-box retrieval in agentic RAG systems
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 diverse QA benchmarks with consistent improvements (22.5% relative EM gain on Qwen3-8B, 36.4% on Musique)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of interaction primitives, SFT, and RL components; valuable training-free scenario evaluation
Practical lightweight implementation leveraging existing infrastructure (SQLite FTS, ChromaDB) making the approach deployable and efficient
Strong generalization to both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, with only 4.8K trajectories for SFT
Detailed reproducibility support including complete prompts, implementation details, and promised corpus release
Insightful analysis of interaction patterns across training stages (Figure 5) showing emergence of learned strategies
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines well-established techniques (semantic + exact search fusion, entity matching, document filtering, standard SFT+RL training) rather than introducing novel methods or theoretical insights

Experimental fairness concerns: different LLM backbones for baselines (Qwen2.5-7B for training-based methods vs. Qwen3-8B main), differential thinking mode usage, and curated corpus construction that may not reflect real-world distribution
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: limited investigation of why these specific action categories help or which questions benefit from which primitives; 'Reflect & Refine' mechanism underexplored
Evaluation limited to QA tasks only; generalization to other RAG applications (summarization, open-ended generation) unclear; no human evaluation or failure case analysis

Corpus construction artifacts: different treatment across benchmarks (metadata-based vs. synthetic queries) creates curated rather than realistic retrieval scenarios; questions about generalization to truly out-of-distribution corpora
Missing efficiency analysis: action iterations reported but not wall-clock time or token costs compared to baselines
No systematic exploration of alternative interaction primitive sets or comparison with other hybrid retrieval approaches widely used in production
Technical design choices inadequately justified: simple reward function, GRPO specifics, why these three action categories, masking rationale

strengths: Clear problem identification: articulates a genuine limitation of black-box retrieval in agentic RAG—agents resort to inefficient query reformulation loops. The motivating example is concrete and compelling.

Well-designed practical solution: three categories of interaction primitives (multi-faceted retrieval, anchored matching, context shaping) comprehensively address the identified limitations with lightweight implementation using existing tools.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: six diverse benchmarks (both single-hop and multi-hop), appropriate baselines including recent methods, and strong consistent improvements (22.5% relative gain over Search-R1, 36.4% on Musique).

Thorough ablation studies: clear evidence for interaction paradigm (8.9-21.9% drops), necessity of both SFT and RL phases, effectiveness even without training (Table 3), and efficiency analysis showing fewer action iterations.

Insightful analysis: Figure 5 shows how agents learn to use different action types across training stages; Figure 6 case study clearly demonstrates advantages; training dynamics analysis explains two-stage training superiority.
Strong reproducibility: comprehensive implementation details, full prompts for all components, plans to release corpus, and detailed experimental setup.
Clear presentation: well-organized paper with effective figures, intuitive examples, and good balance between main narrative and supplementary materials.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: multi-faceted retrieval and hybrid search are well-established; reasoning-enhanced workflow (planner-reasoner-executor) combines standard decomposition ideas; GRPO is from prior work. Main novelty is integration rather than fundamental technical innovation.

Corpus construction concerns: custom-built corpus leverages benchmark metadata (candidate passages), which is somewhat oracle-like. Raises fairness concerns; limits assessment on completely novel corpora. Mitigated by out-of-distribution benchmarks but still a limitation.

Model size inconsistency in primary results: Table 1 mixes different model sizes (Qwen3-8B vs 7B for baselines). Though Table 4 addresses this, primary results lack clarity. Makes direct comparison less clean than ideal.

Insufficient computational cost analysis: no discussion of overhead from multiple LLM calls in reasoning-enhanced workflow (planner, reasoner, executor). No timing comparisons with baselines. Critical for practical deployment assessment but missing.

Training data disparity: uses 4.8K trajectories (SFT) and 7.1K QA pairs (RL), while Search-R1 uses 170K QA pairs. Though noted in appendix, unclear whether improvements stem from the method or data efficiency. Comparable training budgets would strengthen claims.

Shallow analysis of when interactions help: limited investigation of which query types benefit from which primitives; no systematic failure case analysis; doesn't discuss scenarios where interaction paradigm may not provide benefits.

Generalization claims somewhat overstated: trains on 3 datasets, evaluates on 6, but only 3 are truly out-of-distribution. All datasets are Wikipedia-based. Claim of 'great generalization' could be more carefully qualified.
Limited evaluation scope: only extractive QA with EM/F1 metrics; no generation-based QA or diverse tasks; all datasets Wikipedia-based; no user studies or qualitative evaluation of reasoning quality.

Simple reward function design: RL reward is quite basic (R(τ) = -1 + validity + accuracy). More sophisticated reward shaping (e.g., information gain, retrieval quality) unexplored. Limited discussion of alternative designs.

Missing discussion of practical limitations: insufficient treatment of what interaction types matter most, when the approach struggles, how it scales with corpus size, and other practical considerations.

strengths: Clear problem identification: effectively motivates the limitation of black-box retrieval in existing agentic RAG systems with concrete examples
Strong empirical results: 22.5% relative improvement over second-best method with pronounced gains on complex multi-hop QA (36.4% on MuSiQue)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: six benchmarks with diverse baselines, extensive ablations, training dynamics analysis, and generalization assessment with limited training data (12K vs 170K)
Well-designed interaction primitives: intuitive categorization into multi-faceted retrieval, anchored matching, and context shaping with clear implementability
Excellent reproducibility: detailed documentation, code commitment, comprehensive appendices with prompts and training details, and supporting fact coverage evaluation
Insightful analysis: Figures 4-5 effectively demonstrate training dynamics and learned retrieval strategies (e.g., RL-induced preference for entity matching)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines known techniques (semantic+exact search fusion, standard SFT+RL, straightforward task decomposition). Main contribution is application rather than fundamental innovation

Significant computational overhead: 2.1× higher latency (36.4s vs 17.2s) and 3.7× higher token usage compared to Search-R1, potentially prohibitive for real-world deployment despite frame as test-time scaling trade-off

Questionable experimental fairness: paper constructs corpus using benchmark metadata and synthetic query generation for missing evidence, potentially systematically favoring Interact-RAG over query-only baselines on curated rather than generic corpora
Comparison inconsistencies: uses 7B models for key baselines (Search-R1, R-Search, S-DeepSearcher) while testing Interact-RAG-8B, undermining direct comparison validity

Dependence on stronger model for synthesis: uses Qwen-Plus to generate 4.8K training trajectories, creating unequal advantage for Interact-RAG and confounding whether gains stem from interaction paradigm vs superior synthetic data

Task-dependent primitive utility: Table 3 shows different primitives critical for different datasets (Multi-Faceted Retrieval for 2Wiki, Context Shaping for MuSiQue), suggesting method lacks universal robustness across question types
Simple reward function: outcome-based only without process rewards; papers acknowledges this limitation and suggests advanced RL as future work
Insufficient error analysis: lacks systematic analysis of failure cases and when Interact-RAG still struggles, limiting understanding of method applicability boundaries
Presentation issues: Table reference error ('Table ??'), dense simultaneous introduction of multiple components, and unclear implementation details (e.g., how agent learns primitive preferences)
Training component balance: Table 2 shows SFT drops (-21.9% on Musique) exceed RL drops (-16.9%), questioning incremental value of RL optimization phase

strengths: Clear problem identification and well-motivated solution addressing a real limitation in black-box RAG systems
Strong empirical results across six benchmarks with 22.5% relative improvement over the second-best method, particularly impressive on multi-hop QA (36.4% on MuSiQue)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablations (interaction paradigm, individual primitives, training components), training-free scenarios, and detailed analysis of retrieval efficiency and training dynamics
Excellent generalization demonstrated across both in-distribution (NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (PopQA, 2Wiki, Bamboogle)
Efficient use of training data - achieves strong results with 12K QA pairs versus 170K for competitive baselines
Thorough reproducibility support with detailed implementation documentation, comprehensive appendices with prompts, and promised code release
Well-presented paper with clear motivation, effective visualizations, insightful case studies, and systematic ablation analyses
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - individual components (semantic/exact search, entity matching, doc filtering, hierarchical reasoning, GRPO) are well-established techniques; primary contribution is in combination and application rather than fundamental innovations

Significant practical limitations from computational overhead - 2.1× higher latency (36.4s vs 17.2s) and 3.7× higher token consumption (713 vs 192), raising concerns about real-world deployment feasibility

Experimental setup concerns including corpus modification to match QA benchmarks (advantage to Interact-RAG), use of synthetic queries for Bamboogle corpus construction, different model versions across comparisons (Qwen3-8B vs Qwen2.5-7B), and asymmetric data preprocessing
Insufficient analysis of when and why each interaction primitive is beneficial - no breakdown by question type or deeper investigation of primitive interactions beyond aggregate ablations

Training data quality and scalability not thoroughly examined - only 4.8K filtered trajectories, filtering of 'simplistic' questions could introduce bias, and unclear how approach transfers to other domains
Limited evaluation scope - only QA tasks evaluated; generalization to other retrieval-dependent tasks (summarization, fact verification) remains unclear
Relatively simple outcome-based RL reward function with limited exploration of process rewards; -1 penalty appears arbitrary as it cancels in GRPO normalization
Missing human evaluation of trajectory quality and reasoning coherence; evaluation relies solely on EM/F1 scores without assessing actual quality of information-seeking strategies
